title: HTTP HTTPS TLS certificates HSTS and transport security
concepts: HTTP is an application protocol; TLS protects a transport connection and authenticates the server, while HTTPS is HTTP carried over TLS. Security must cover the whole request path, not only login.
TLS certificates bind public keys to identities through trust anchors. Expiry, hostname mismatch, incomplete chains, weak settings, and private-key exposure are separate failures.

HSTS is a browser policy learned from HTTPS that tells future connections to use HTTPS. It complements secure deployment and redirects; it does not protect the first visit unless the domain is preloaded.
When TLS terminates at a reverse proxy, forwarded scheme and client metadata are trustworthy only from configured proxy addresses.

RFC 9846 is a July 2026 Standards Track Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 8446 while retaining TLS version 1.3. It prohibits TLS 1.0/1.1 negotiation, prohibits KeyShare reuse between connections, clarifies PSK/HelloRetryRequest hash selection, requires ignoring NewSessionTicket when resumption is unsupported, and strengthens KeyUpdate requirements.

RFC 9849 standardizes Encrypted Client Hello; RFC 9848 defines the DNS HTTPS/SVCB ech parameter. ECH rejection yields only public-name authentication, must not be reported as origin success or used for application data, and follows defined retry/error rules. Mixed ECH/non-ECH DNS endpoints can permit downgrade.
RFC 9525 defines current TLS service identity verification: use typed subjectAltName identifiers, do not fall back to Common Name, and constrain DNS wildcards to the complete left-most label.
TLS 1.3 0-RTT is replayable, must be explicitly enabled for application use, and requires distributed anti-replay safeguards or should remain disabled.
